chapter_sections.label: DEFINITION:
chapter_sections.text: Control and coordination refer to the mechanisms by which living organisms detect changes in their environment (stimuli) and produce appropriate responses to those changes. In multicellular organisms, specialised tissues provide these control and coordination activities.

chapter_sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: All living organisms respond to changes in their environment.
Movement in organisms can be a response to stimuli (e.g., touch, light, gravity).
Some movements are caused by growth; others are independent of growth.
In animals, control and coordination are provided by the nervous system and hormones.
In plants, control and coordination occur through chemical signals (plant hormones) and electrical-chemical communication between cells.
The two systems of control and coordination in animals are the NERVOUS SYSTEM and the ENDOCRINE (HORMONAL) SYSTEM.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: The nervous system in animals consists of specialised cells called NEURONS (nerve cells) that detect information from the environment, process it, and transmit responses to muscles and glands through electrical impulses.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Receptors are specialised tips of nerve cells that detect stimuli; they are located in sense organs (inner ear, nose, tongue, etc.).
A NEURON has three main parts: DENDRITES (receive information), CELL BODY (processes information), and AXON (transmits impulse to next neuron or effector).
Information acquired at the dendritic tip creates an ELECTRICAL IMPULSE that travels from dendrite to cell body to axon.
At the end of the axon, the electrical impulse causes release of CHEMICALS (neurotransmitters) that cross the GAP (SYNAPSE) and start a similar impulse in the next neuron.
A SYNAPSE is the tiny gap between two neurons where chemical transmission of impulse takes place.
The final synapse allows delivery of impulses from neurons to other cells such as MUSCLE CELLS or GLANDS.
Nervous tissue is made up of an organised network of nerve cells (neurons) specialised for conducting information via electrical impulses from one part of the body to another.
GUSTATORY RECEPTORS detect taste; OLFACTORY RECEPTORS detect smell.
Figure 6.1 (a) shows the structure of a neuron (nucleus, dendrite, cell body, axon, nerve ending); Figure 6.1 (b) shows the neuromuscular junction.
IN-TEXT QUESTION (Figure 6.1):
Look at Fig. 6.1 (a) and identify the parts of a neuron:
(i) where information is acquired,
(ii) through which information travels as an electrical impulse, and
(iii) where this impulse must be converted into a chemical signal for onward transmission.

[Answers: (i) Dendrite tip - information acquired here from environment/other neurons; (ii) Axon - electrical impulse travels along the axon; (iii) Axon end/nerve ending - here the electrical impulse is converted into a chemical signal (neurotransmitter) that crosses the synapse to the next neuron or effector.]

sections.label: ACTIVITY 6.1:
sections.aim: To understand how taste perception is linked to smell.
sections.materials: Sugar, nose (to be blocked with fingers).
procedure: 1. Put some sugar in your mouth and note how it tastes.
2. Block your nose by pressing it between your thumb and index finger. Eat sugar again and note the difference in taste.
3. While eating lunch, block your nose in the same way and notice if you can fully appreciate the taste of the food.
sections.observation: When the nose is blocked, the taste of sugar and food changes - it is less distinct or less pleasant.
sections.conclusion:
Taste perception is closely linked to smell. Gustatory and olfactory receptors together contribute to the sense of taste. When smell is blocked, taste experience is diminished.

items.question: What is a neuron? Name its three main parts.
items.answer:
A NEURON is the structural and functional unit of the nervous system. It is a specialised cell that carries electrical impulses from one part of the body to another.
Three main parts of a neuron:
1. DENDRITES - receive information/impulses from the environment or other neurons.
2. CELL BODY - contains the nucleus and processes the information.
3. AXON - transmits the impulse away from the cell body to the next neuron or effector.

items.question: What is a synapse? What is its role in nerve impulse transmission?
items.answer:
A SYNAPSE is the tiny gap or junction between the axon end of one neuron and the dendrite of the next neuron.
Role: When an electrical impulse reaches the end of the axon, it triggers the release of CHEMICALS (neurotransmitters). These chemicals cross the synapse and start a similar electrical impulse in the dendrite of the next neuron. The synapse thus allows nerve impulse transmission from one neuron to another through chemical signals.

items.question: Describe the structure of a neuron with the help of a labelled diagram (describe).
items.answer:
A NEURON consists of:
1. CELL BODY (Cyton): Contains the nucleus and cytoplasm; it processes information.
2. DENDRITES: Short, branching projections from the cell body that receive impulses from other neurons or sense organs.
3. AXON: A long, slender projection that carries impulses away from the cell body to the next neuron or to a muscle/gland.
4. NERVE ENDINGS: The terminal branches of the axon that form synapses with the next neuron or with muscle fibres (neuromuscular junction).
The electrical impulse travels: Dendrite -> Cell body -> Axon -> Synapse -> Next neuron/effector.

items.question: What is a reflex action? Explain with the help of a reflex arc.
items.answer:
REFLEX ACTION: A reflex action is a sudden, automatic, and involuntary response to a stimulus that occurs without conscious thought. It is the quickest response to an urgent stimulus.
Example: Pulling the hand away from a hot object.

REFLEX ARC: The pathway through which a nerve impulse travels during a reflex action is called a REFLEX ARC.
Pathway of reflex arc (for touching a hot object):
1. RECEPTOR (heat/pain receptors in skin) detects the stimulus (heat).
2. SENSORY NEURON carries the impulse from receptor to spinal cord (CNS).
3. RELAY NEURON in the spinal cord processes and relays the impulse.
4. MOTOR NEURON carries the impulse from spinal cord to the effector.
5. EFFECTOR (muscle in arm) responds by contracting - hand is pulled away.
The information input also goes on to reach the brain simultaneously, but the response is completed at the spinal cord level before the brain even registers it.

items.question: Describe the structure and functions of the human brain.
items.answer:
The HUMAN BRAIN is the main coordinating centre of the body. It is located in the skull (cranium) and constitutes the CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM (CNS) along with the spinal cord.
The brain has three major parts:
1. FORE-BRAIN (Cerebrum):
- Main thinking part of the brain.
- Receives and interprets sensory impulses (sight, smell, hearing, etc.).
- Controls voluntary actions and stores memory.
- Contains a centre associated with hunger.
2. MID-BRAIN:
- Controls involuntary actions like pupil size, eye movement.
3. HIND-BRAIN:
- CEREBELLUM: Controls precision of voluntary actions and maintains posture and balance.
- MEDULLA: Controls involuntary actions like blood pressure, salivation, vomiting, and heartbeat.
- PONS: Part of the hind-brain.
The brain receives information from all parts of the body and integrates it to produce appropriate responses.

items.question: Explain how the nervous system controls and coordinates actions in the human body. Distinguish between voluntary, involuntary, and reflex actions.
items.answer:
The NERVOUS SYSTEM controls and coordinates body actions through a network of neurons that transmit electrical impulses.

HOW IT WORKS:
1. RECEPTORS in sense organs detect stimuli from the environment.
2. SENSORY NEURONS carry these impulses to the CNS (brain or spinal cord).
3. The CNS processes the information and decides the response.
4. MOTOR NEURONS carry the response impulse to effectors (muscles/glands).
5. EFFECTORS (muscles/glands) produce the actual response or movement.

TYPES OF ACTIONS:

1. VOLUNTARY ACTIONS:
- Controlled by the fore-brain (cerebrum).
- Require conscious thought and decision.
- Example: Writing, talking, picking up a pencil.
- These are deliberate actions.

2. INVOLUNTARY ACTIONS:
- Controlled by the mid-brain and hind-brain (medulla, cerebellum).
- Do not require conscious control - they happen automatically.
- Example: Heartbeat, breathing, blood pressure regulation, salivation, vomiting.
- These cannot be easily controlled by thinking.

3. REFLEX ACTIONS:
- The fastest type of response; controlled at the level of the SPINAL CORD (not brain).
- Happen without thinking - automatic response to sudden stimulus.
- Pathway: Receptor -> Sensory neuron -> Spinal cord (relay neuron) -> Motor neuron -> Effector.
- Example: Pulling hand from fire, blinking when something comes near the eye.
- Reflex arcs have evolved for quick, efficient responses when brain processing would be too slow.

KEY DIFFERENCE: Voluntary actions are thought-out; involuntary actions are automatic but brain-controlled; reflex actions bypass the brain and are spinal cord-controlled.

items.question: The part of the neuron that receives information from the environment is:
items.explanation: Dendrites are the branching projections that receive stimuli or impulses and pass them to the cell body. The axon transmits impulses away from the cell body; the synapse is the gap between neurons.

items.question: What is the gap between two neurons called?
items.explanation: The synapse is the tiny gap between the axon end of one neuron and the dendrite of the next. Nerve impulse crosses this gap via chemical neurotransmitters, not electrically.

items.question: Which part of the brain controls posture and balance of the body?
items.explanation: The cerebellum (part of hind-brain) controls precision of voluntary actions and maintains posture and balance. Medulla controls involuntary actions; cerebrum controls thinking and voluntary actions.

items.question: In a reflex arc, the order of transmission of nerve impulse is:

options.A: Receptor -> Motor neuron -> Spinal cord -> Sensory neuron -> Effector
options.B: Receptor -> Sensory neuron -> Spinal cord -> Motor neuron -> Effector
options.C: Receptor -> Spinal cord -> Sensory neuron -> Motor neuron -> Effector
options.D: Effector -> Sensory neuron -> Spinal cord -> Motor neuron -> Receptor

items.explanation: In a reflex arc, the impulse travels from receptor through sensory neuron to spinal cord (CNS), then through motor neuron to the effector (muscle). This bypasses the brain for speed.

items.question: Which of the following is a reflex action?

options.B: Pulling hand away from a flame

items.explanation: Pulling the hand away from a flame is a sudden, automatic response to pain/heat stimulus - a reflex action. The other options (writing, cycling, talking) are voluntary actions requiring conscious thought.

items.question: Blood pressure, salivation and vomiting are controlled by which part of the brain?
items.explanation: The medulla (in hind-brain) controls involuntary actions like blood pressure, salivation, and vomiting. Cerebellum controls balance and posture; cerebrum controls voluntary actions and thinking.

items.question: A person's spinal cord is injured in an accident. Which of the following would most likely be affected?
items.explanation: Reflex arcs are formed in the spinal cord. A spinal cord injury would disrupt reflex actions. Thinking and memory are controlled by the cerebrum (fore-brain); smell by olfactory receptors connected to fore-brain.

items.question: Why do reflex arcs exist even in animals with complex brains?

options.A: Because the brain cannot process any information
options.B: Because reflex arcs are more accurate than brain responses
options.C: Because reflex arcs provide faster responses than brain-mediated responses
options.D: Because involuntary actions do not need a nervous system

items.explanation: Reflex arcs bypass the brain and are processed at the spinal cord level, making the response much faster than waiting for brain processing. In emergencies (like touching hot objects), speed is critical to prevent injury.

items.question: What is the difference between a reflex action and walking?
items.answer:
A: A REFLEX ACTION is a sudden, automatic response to a stimulus that is controlled at the spinal cord level (does not involve conscious brain control). It happens without thinking. Example: pulling hand from a hot object.
WALKING is a VOLUNTARY ACTION controlled by the fore-brain (cerebrum). It requires conscious thought, planning, and coordination of many muscles. The brain decides to walk, sends signals to leg muscles, and the cerebellum coordinates precise movement and balance. Walking can be started or stopped at will; reflex actions cannot.

items.question: What happens at the synapse between two neurons?
items.answer:
A: At the synapse (gap between two neurons), the following happens:
1. An electrical impulse travelling along the axon of the first neuron reaches the axon end/nerve ending.
2. The electrical impulse cannot directly cross the synapse.
3. The impulse triggers the release of CHEMICAL substances (neurotransmitters) from the axon end of the first neuron.
4. These chemicals diffuse across the synapse.
5. They bind to the dendrite of the next neuron.
6. This starts a new ELECTRICAL IMPULSE in the second neuron.
Thus, at the synapse, electrical transmission is converted to chemical transmission and back to electrical transmission.

items.question: Which part of the brain maintains posture and equilibrium of the body?
items.answer: A: The CEREBELLUM (part of the hind-brain) maintains posture and equilibrium (balance) of the body. It is also responsible for precision of voluntary actions such as walking in a straight line, riding a bicycle, and picking up objects.

items.question: How do we detect the smell of an agarbatti (incense stick)?
items.answer: A: When an agarbatti burns, it releases chemical molecules into the air. These molecules reach our nose when we breathe in. Inside the nose, OLFACTORY RECEPTORS (specialised tip cells of certain nerve cells) detect these chemical molecules. The receptors are stimulated and generate an electrical impulse. This impulse travels along olfactory nerves to the fore-brain (cerebrum). The fore-brain interprets the impulse by comparing it with stored information and we identify it as the smell of agarbatti.

items.question: What is the role of the brain in reflex action?
items.answer: A: In a reflex action, the brain does NOT control the immediate response - the response is completed at the SPINAL CORD level through the reflex arc (receptor -> sensory neuron -> spinal cord -> motor neuron -> effector). However, the brain does play a role simultaneously: the information input also travels from the spinal cord UP to the brain. The brain receives and registers the stimulus (e.g., we feel the pain from touching a hot object a moment after our hand has already moved). The brain thus becomes AWARE of the reflex action after it has happened, but does not initiate or control it.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: A REFLEX ACTION is a sudden, automatic, involuntary response to a stimulus that is accomplished without conscious thought. It is controlled at the level of the spinal cord through a pathway called a REFLEX ARC.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Common examples of reflex expressions: "I jumped out of the way of the bus reflexly", "I pulled my hand back from the flame reflexly", "my mouth started watering reflexly."
All these involve doing something without thinking, yet they are responses to environmental changes.
Thinking involves complex interaction of many nerve impulses from many neurons - this takes time.
The body solves the speed problem by connecting the input nerve (detecting heat) directly to the output nerve (moving muscles) at the SPINAL CORD level - this is a REFLEX ARC.
REFLEX ARC: Input nerve (sensory neuron) -> Relay neuron in spinal cord -> Output nerve (motor neuron) -> Muscle (effector).
Nerves from all over the body meet in a bundle in the SPINAL CORD on their way to the brain. Reflex arcs are formed in this spinal cord.
The information input also goes on to reach the brain (we feel the pain slightly later).
Reflex arcs have evolved in animals because the thinking process of the brain is not fast enough for urgent situations.
Even after complex neuron networks evolved, reflex arcs continue to be more efficient for quick responses.

FIGURE 6.2 shows the reflex arc: Receptors (heat/pain in skin) -> Sensory neuron -> Spinal cord (CNS) with Relay neuron -> Motor neuron -> Effector (muscle in arm); a message is also sent to the brain.
IN-TEXT QUESTION (Figure 6.2):
Can you now trace the sequence of events which occur when a bright light is focussed on your eyes?

[Answer: 1. Light receptors in the eye (retina) detect bright light. 2. Electrical impulse travels via sensory neuron to spinal cord/brain. 3. The response (pupil constriction) - muscles of the iris contract to reduce pupil size. This is an involuntary action controlled by the mid-brain. The sequence: Light stimulus -> Retinal receptors -> Sensory neuron -> Brain (mid-brain) -> Motor neuron -> Iris muscles -> Pupil constricts.]

items.question: What is a reflex arc? Name the components in the correct order.
items.answer:
A REFLEX ARC is the pathway through which a nerve impulse travels during a reflex action, from the receptor to the effector, passing through the spinal cord.
Components in order:
Receptor -> Sensory neuron -> Spinal cord (relay neuron) -> Motor neuron -> Effector (muscle/gland)

items.question: Why is a reflex action so fast? Explain the advantage of reflex arcs over brain-mediated responses.
items.answer:
A reflex action is so fast because the nerve impulse does NOT travel all the way to the brain for processing. Instead, it is processed at the SPINAL CORD level through a reflex arc.
Reason for speed:
- Brain-mediated responses require: Receptor -> Sensory neuron -> Brain -> Motor neuron -> Effector. This takes more time.
- Reflex responses only need: Receptor -> Sensory neuron -> Spinal cord -> Motor neuron -> Effector. The pathway is much shorter.
Advantage: In dangerous situations (touching a hot object, stepping on a sharp object), the response must be immediate to prevent injury. Waiting for brain processing could cause serious harm. Reflex arcs provide the fastest possible response. Even animals with little brain capacity can protect themselves through reflex arcs.

items.question: With the help of a labelled description of a reflex arc, explain what happens when you accidentally touch a hot object.
items.answer:
When you accidentally touch a hot object:
1. RECEPTOR: Heat/pain receptors in the skin detect the stimulus (heat from the hot object).
2. SENSORY NEURON: Carries the nerve impulse from the receptor to the spinal cord.
3. RELAY NEURON in SPINAL CORD: Receives the impulse, processes it, and passes it to the motor neuron. Simultaneously, a message is sent to the brain (this is why you feel pain a moment later).
4. MOTOR NEURON: Carries the impulse from the spinal cord to the effector (muscle in the arm).
5. EFFECTOR (Muscle): The arm muscle contracts and the hand is immediately pulled away from the hot object.
The entire response (steps 1-5) happens BEFORE the brain even receives and registers the pain. This is why we withdraw our hand almost instantly - faster than we can consciously "decide" to do so.
Path: Receptor (skin) -> Sensory neuron -> Spinal cord -> Motor neuron -> Muscle (effector)

items.question: Which part of the CNS forms reflex arcs?
items.explanation: Reflex arcs are formed in the spinal cord. Nerves from all over the body meet in the spinal cord, and the reflex response is completed here without involving the brain.

items.question: In a reflex action, which type of neuron carries impulse from the spinal cord to the muscle?
items.explanation: The motor neuron carries the impulse from the spinal cord (CNS) to the effector (muscle). Sensory neuron carries impulse TO the spinal cord; relay neuron is within the spinal cord.

items.question: What is the correct pathway of a reflex arc?

options.A: Effector -> Motor neuron -> CNS -> Sensory neuron -> Receptor
options.B: Receptor -> Motor neuron -> CNS -> Sensory neuron -> Effector
options.C: Receptor -> Sensory neuron -> CNS -> Motor neuron -> Effector
options.D: CNS -> Sensory neuron -> Receptor -> Motor neuron -> Effector

items.explanation: The correct reflex arc pathway is: Receptor detects stimulus -> Sensory neuron carries to CNS -> CNS (spinal cord) processes -> Motor neuron carries to effector -> Effector responds.

items.question: When you touch a hot plate, your hand pulls away before you consciously feel the pain. This is because:

options.A: Pain receptors are located in the brain
options.B: The reflex arc bypasses the brain and is completed at the spinal cord
options.C: The brain processes information faster than the spinal cord
options.D: The motor neuron sends signals directly to the brain

items.explanation: The reflex arc is completed at the spinal cord level before the brain registers the pain. The hand withdraws almost instantly as the response is not waiting for brain processing.

items.question: If the sensory neuron connecting the spinal cord to the brain is damaged but the reflex arc is intact, what would happen when a person touches a hot object?

options.A: The hand would not withdraw at all
options.B: The hand would withdraw but the person would not feel pain
options.C: The person would feel pain but the hand would not withdraw
options.D: Neither withdrawal nor pain perception would occur

items.explanation: The reflex arc (receptor -> sensory neuron -> spinal cord -> motor neuron -> muscle) is still intact, so the hand withdraws automatically. However, since the sensory neuron to the brain is damaged, the pain signal never reaches the brain and the person does not consciously feel pain.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: The HUMAN BRAIN is the main coordinating centre of the body. It sits inside the skull (cranium) and, along with the spinal cord, constitutes the CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM (CNS). The brain receives information from all parts of the body, integrates it, and produces appropriate responses.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: The brain and spinal cord together form the CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM (CNS).
The PERIPHERAL NERVOUS SYSTEM consists of cranial nerves (arising from the brain) and spinal nerves (arising from the spinal cord). It connects the CNS to all other parts of the body.
The brain has three major parts: FORE-BRAIN, MID-BRAIN, and HIND-BRAIN.
FORE-BRAIN (Cerebrum):
Main thinking part of the brain.
Has regions that receive sensory impulses from various receptors (hearing, smell, sight, etc.).
Separate areas of association interpret sensory information by combining it with information from other receptors and stored memory.
Motor areas control voluntary muscle movement.
A separate centre is associated with HUNGER.
MID-BRAIN: Controls involuntary actions like change in pupil size and eye movement.
HIND-BRAIN has three parts:
CEREBELLUM: Controls precision of voluntary actions; maintains posture and balance of the body. Activities like walking straight, riding a bicycle, and picking up a pencil require cerebellum.
MEDULLA: Controls involuntary actions including blood pressure, salivation, and vomiting.
PONS: Connects different parts of the brain; involved in breathing regulation.
FIGURE 6.3 shows the labelled human brain: Cerebrum (fore-brain), Hypothalamus, Pituitary gland, Mid-brain, Pons, Medulla, Cerebellum (hind-brain), Spinal cord.
IN-TEXT QUESTION (Figure 6.3):
Study the labelled diagram of the human brain (Fig. 6.3). We have seen that the different parts have specific functions. Can we find out the function of each part?
[Answer:
CEREBRUM (Fore-brain): Thinking, reasoning, memory, interpretation of sensory impulses (sight, smell, hearing), voluntary muscle control, hunger centre.
HYPOTHALAMUS: Regulates body temperature, hunger, thirst; controls pituitary gland through releasing factors.
PITUITARY GLAND: Master gland - secretes growth hormone and other hormones; attached below hypothalamus.
MID-BRAIN: Controls involuntary actions like pupil size and eye movement.
PONS (Hind-brain): Connects brain regions; involved in breathing regulation.
MEDULLA (Hind-brain): Controls vital involuntary actions - blood pressure, salivation, vomiting.
CEREBELLUM (Hind-brain): Precision of voluntary actions, posture, balance.
SPINAL CORD: Information highway between brain and body; contains reflex arcs.]

items.question: What is the central nervous system? Name its two components.
items.answer:
The CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM (CNS) is the main control and coordination centre of the body that receives, processes, and integrates information from all parts of the body.
Two components of CNS:
1. BRAIN - located in the skull (cranium).
2. SPINAL CORD - runs through the vertebral column (backbone).

items.question: Name the three regions of the hind-brain and state the function of each.
items.answer:
Three regions of hind-brain:
1. CEREBELLUM: Controls precision of voluntary actions and maintains posture and balance of the body.
2. MEDULLA: Controls involuntary actions such as blood pressure, salivation, and vomiting.
3. PONS: Connects different parts of the brain and helps regulate breathing.

items.question: What is the role of the fore-brain in the human body?
items.answer:
The FORE-BRAIN (Cerebrum) is the main thinking part of the brain. Its roles include:
1. SENSORY INTEGRATION: It has regions that receive sensory impulses from various receptors - for hearing, smell, sight, and other senses. Separate areas of association interpret this information by combining it with information stored in memory.
2. MOTOR CONTROL: Motor areas of the fore-brain control the movement of voluntary muscles (e.g., our leg muscles, arm muscles).
3. HIGHER FUNCTIONS: It is responsible for thinking, reasoning, memory, and decision-making.
4. HUNGER CENTRE: A separate part of the fore-brain is associated with hunger, helping us know when we have eaten enough.
The fore-brain is the most developed part of the human brain, reflecting our complex cognitive abilities.

items.question: Distinguish between voluntary, involuntary, and reflex actions with examples. Which part of the brain/CNS controls each?
items.answer:
1. VOLUNTARY ACTIONS:
- Definition: Deliberate, conscious actions that require thinking and decision-making.
- Control: Fore-brain (Cerebrum).
- Examples: Writing, talking, picking up a pencil, walking towards a destination.

2. INVOLUNTARY ACTIONS:
- Definition: Automatic actions that occur without conscious control; the organism cannot easily start or stop them by thinking.
- Control: Mid-brain and Hind-brain (Medulla, Cerebellum).
- Examples: Heartbeat, breathing, blood pressure regulation, salivation, digestion.

3. REFLEX ACTIONS:
- Definition: Sudden, automatic responses to stimuli that are completed before the brain processes the stimulus. They are the fastest type of response.
- Control: SPINAL CORD (through reflex arcs).
- Examples: Pulling hand from hot object, blinking when a bright light is focused on eyes, knee-jerk reaction.

KEY DIFFERENCE: Voluntary = brain (conscious); Involuntary = brain (unconscious); Reflex = spinal cord (bypass brain).

items.question: What is the role of the cerebellum? What would happen if the cerebellum is damaged?
items.answer:
ROLE OF CEREBELLUM:
The CEREBELLUM (part of hind-brain) is responsible for:
1. PRECISION OF VOLUNTARY ACTIONS: It fine-tunes voluntary movements so they are smooth, accurate, and coordinated.
2. POSTURE AND BALANCE: It maintains the posture and balance of the body at all times.
3. COORDINATION OF MOVEMENT: Activities like walking in a straight line, riding a bicycle, picking up a pencil, and playing sports all require the cerebellum to coordinate muscle movements.

IF CEREBELLUM IS DAMAGED:
- The person would lose balance and fall easily.
- Voluntary movements would become jerky, uncoordinated, and inaccurate (a condition called ATAXIA).
- Simple activities like walking, writing, or picking up objects would become very difficult.
- The person would be unable to ride a bicycle or perform tasks requiring precise muscle control.
The person can still think and feel (fore-brain is intact) and basic life functions would continue (medulla intact), but coordination of movement would be severely impaired.

items.question: Describe the structure of the human brain with a labelled description. Explain how different parts work together to control body functions.
items.answer:
STRUCTURE OF HUMAN BRAIN:
The human brain is divided into three major regions: Fore-brain, Mid-brain, and Hind-brain.

1. FORE-BRAIN (Cerebrum):
- Largest and most developed part of the brain.
- Located at the front of the skull.
- Parts: Cerebrum, Hypothalamus (regulates body temperature, hunger, thirst).
- Functions: Thinking, reasoning, memory, voluntary movement, interpretation of sensory impulses (sight, smell, hearing), hunger regulation.

2. MID-BRAIN:
- Located between the fore-brain and hind-brain.
- Controls involuntary actions: pupil size change, eye movement.
- Relays information between fore-brain and hind-brain.

3. HIND-BRAIN:
- Located at the back and lower part of the brain, connecting to the spinal cord.
- Three parts:
a. CEREBELLUM: Precision of voluntary actions, posture, balance.
b. MEDULLA: Controls vital involuntary functions - blood pressure, salivation, vomiting.
c. PONS: Connects brain regions; involved in breathing regulation.

HOW PARTS WORK TOGETHER:
- When you see a ball coming towards you (voluntary action response):
* Fore-brain receives and interprets the visual stimulus, decides to catch the ball.
* Motor cortex of fore-brain sends voluntary signals to arm muscles.
* Cerebellum coordinates the precise muscle movements needed to catch.
* Medulla ensures heartbeat and breathing continue normally throughout.
- When you accidentally touch a hot object (reflex):
* Spinal cord handles the immediate reflex withdrawal.
* Brain receives the pain signal slightly later and registers it.
- Brain and spinal cord communicate constantly through the peripheral nervous system (cranial and spinal nerves) to maintain all body functions.
